title: One soul
hookLine: He created you from a single soul and made its mate, so respect the wombs that bore you (4:1)

cards: At a great many Muslim weddings, before the vows, someone stands and gives a short sermon that the Prophet ﷺ used to open important speeches. It quotes three verses.
One is the first verse of the fourth surah, an-Nisa, the Women. So as two families are being joined, the room hears a verse about where all families came from.
Today, that verse, and a new surah that will spend a long time on family, inheritance and fairness.

teach.b: Surah 4 opens by speaking to everyone: O mankind. Then, in Pickthall's words, be careful of your duty to your Lord "Who created you from a single soul and from it created its mate."
From those two, He spread abroad many men and women.
One soul: nafs wahida. Before any nation, tribe, language or family name, a single origin. Every person you'll meet today is, in the verse's picture, a relative.
Then a phrase that's easy to pass over: be mindful of God, by whom you ask things of one another, and of the arham.
Arham means wombs, and by extension kinship, the ties of family. And here's the detail.
Rahim, womb, comes from the same root as rahma, mercy, and ar-Rahman, the Most Merciful.
A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari makes the link explicit: the word for womb is taken from the name ar-Rahman, and whoever keeps its ties, God keeps ties with them.
So the surah of the Women begins by placing mothers, wombs and family ties right next to God's own mercy. That's why it fits a wedding.

Two families joining are reminded they were already one, and what they owe each other. In the coming days an-Nisa gets very specific: orphans, inheritance shares, kindness in marriage, neighbors near and far.
It all grows out of this first verse. One soul, many people, ties of mercy between them.

how: Muslims hear 4:1 in the khutbat al-hajah, the Prophet's opening sermon recited at many weddings and Friday sermons, and the verse is a basis for keeping ties of kinship, silat al-rahim, a duty stressed throughout Islamic teaching.

o: each person's own private, separate soul

p: mercy, from the same root as womb

s: womb and mercy share a root in Arabic
rahim and rahma, r-h-m, and a hadith in Bukhari links the womb to the name ar-Rahman.
this verse is often heard at weddings
it is one of the three verses in the khutbat al-hajah, recited before many marriages.

games.q: you're at a Muslim wedding. before the vows, a short sermon quotes three verses. one of them is about what?
o: all people created from a single soul.
the story of a well-known couple.
games.why: 4:1: created from a single soul, and mindful of the ties of the womb. two families are reminded they were already one.

practice: Think of your mother, or whoever carried and raised you; if she has died, or that relationship is hard, simply hold her in mind for a moment, or think of another woman who mothered you. If you pray, you can ask God's mercy for her.
Then widen the circle to the people around you today, strangers included, and remember the verse's claim: from one soul.

wordCard.voice: One soul. Nafs wahida: all people from a single soul and its mate, the opening of an-Nisa, 4:1. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: from one soul. In the verse's picture, every stranger is a relative. See you tomorrow.
